title: Check yourself: Best Practices for ISO-8583 Development

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A refund service takes the amount a merchant typed, 4.35 pounds sterling, as a double and builds field 4 with (long) (amount * 100). In a double, 4.35 * 100 is 434.99999999999994. What does field 4 carry?

options.text: Field 4 is 000000000435, since the cast rounds the product to the nearest whole number of pence
options.says: 11.1: the cast drops the fraction, as 0.29 becoming 28 shows; it does not round

options.text: Field 4 is 000000000434, since the product falls a little short and the cast drops its fraction
options.says: 11.1: as 0.29 * 100 = 28.999999999999996 became 28, the cast keeps the whole part, 434

options.text: The refund is refused, since the cast to long rejects a product that is not a whole number
options.says: 11.1: a cast truncates silently; refusing is what an exact conversion does with an amount finer than the currency

options.text: The refund is refused, since a pound amount with two decimals cannot be held in a long
options.says: 11.1 and unit 3: a long holds minor units, so two decimals are no problem once the amount is in pence

origin.section: 11.1. An Amount Counts Minor Units, and Its Currency Says How Many Make One

questions.stem: A switch averages 2 authorizations a second over the year. Its busiest hour has 72,000, with a burst factor of 4, and the rate stays at that peak for ten minutes. The issuers answer in 0.5 seconds, terminals give up after 30, and the team allowed 10 sessions, ten times the average need. What happens in those ten minutes?

options.text: Requests wait for a free session and many answers come too late, since about 40 need a session at once
options.says: 11.3 and 11.4: 72,000 / 3600 x 4 = 80 a second, x 0.5 s = 40 in flight, four times the 10 sessions, so the wait grows every second and answers come after 30 s

options.text: Requests wait for a free session, but every answer still comes in time, since each holds one for 0.5 s
options.says: 11.3 and 11.4: 10 sessions at 0.5 s serve 20 a second against 80 arriving, so the wait grows until answers are late

options.text: Every request gets a session at once, since 10 sessions are ten times the 1 that the average needs
options.says: 11.3: capacity is sized from the busiest second; the yearly average says nothing about it

options.text: Every request gets a session at once, since about 10 need a session at once in the busiest hour
options.says: 11.3: 10 in flight is the busiest hour's average second (20 a second x 0.5 s); the burst factor makes the peak 80 a second, so 40 are in flight

origin.section: 11.3. Capacity Is Sized From the Busiest Second, and Judged by the Slowest Answers

questions.stem: At the peak your switch handles 200 purchases a second. Its dashboard reports a mean answer time of 0.6 s, a median of 0.25 s and a 99th percentile of 34 s. Terminals give up after 25 s. What follows for the peak?

options.text: About two purchases a second end in a reversal, since at least one answer in a hundred comes after the terminal gave up
options.says: 11.3: the 99th percentile is past the terminal's timeout, so 1% or more of 200 a second have unknown outcomes and are reversed

options.text: About two purchases a second are sent to the issuer twice, since the switch repeats each request the terminal gave up on
options.says: 11.3 and unit 4: a purchase with no answer is reversed, never sent again

options.text: No purchase ends in a reversal, since a mean answer time of 0.6 s is far below the terminal's limit of 25 s
options.says: 11.3: the mean hides the slowest answers; the percentile shows answers past the terminal's timeout

options.text: No purchase ends in a reversal, since a median of 0.25 s shows that half the answers arrive at once
options.says: 11.3: half the answers being fast says nothing about the slowest one in a hundred

origin.section: 11.3. Capacity Is Sized From the Busiest Second, and Judged by the Slowest Answers

questions.stem: A switch shares 120 sessions between issuers P and Q. P gets 100 requests a second and answers in 0.2 s. Q gets 10 a second and, since this morning, answers each one after 20 s. No issuer has a limit of its own. What do P's cardholders see?

options.text: Their answers come late, often after the terminal gave up, since Q's requests fill the sessions
options.says: 11.4: Q alone needs 10 x 20 = 200 sessions, so it fills the pool and P's requests queue behind

options.text: Their answers come at once with 91, since the switch sees that the sessions are taken by Q
options.says: 11.4: an immediate 91 needs a limit per issuer; with one shared pool, P's requests just wait

options.text: Their answers stay as fast as before, since P's host still answers each request in 0.2 s
options.says: 11.4: P's host is healthy, but P's requests wait for a session before they reach it

options.text: Their answers stay as fast as before, since a request for P never waits behind a request for Q
options.says: 11.4: with one pool, requests for every issuer queue for the same sessions

origin.section: 11.4. A Slow Destination Gets a Limit of Its Own, and Past It an Immediate 91

questions.stem: Your switch answers for an issuer when that issuer already has 20 requests in flight. A colleague wants that answer to carry 05, so that terminals stop trying the purchase again. What does an 05 tell the acquirer and the cardholder?

options.text: That the issuer refused the card, since 05 is a decline whoever sends it
options.says: 11.4 and unit 9: 05 is a decision about the card, which the issuer never took; 91 reports that it could not be reached

options.text: That the issuer could not be reached, since the switch sends 05 in the issuer's place
options.says: 11.4: that is what 91 says; 05 says the card was refused

options.text: That the purchase should be tried later, since 05 marks a failure that will pass
options.says: 11.4 and unit 9: a decline is the issuer's decision about the card; only an error such as 91 leaves the cardholder free to try again

options.text: That the purchase should be reversed, since the switch never sent it on
options.says: 11.4: none of the requests answered at once needs a reversal, since none reached the issuer

origin.section: 11.4. A Slow Destination Gets a Limit of Its Own, and Past It an Immediate 91

concepts: The mean hides answers that arrive after the terminal's timeout; the 99th percentile shows them, and each one becomes a reversal.
A double cannot hold most decimal amounts exactly, so a multiply-and-cast loses a minor unit.
Capacity comes from the busiest hour times the burst factor, and in-flight requests are that rate times the answer time.
